results.title: How to Avoid Overfitting and Underfitting in Machine Learning | by ShafaqBibi | Medium
results.content: In machine learning (ML), one of the biggest challenges is ***overfitting,*** which occurs when a model memorizes all the data, including noise and random patterns, without understanding the underlying patterns or logic. As a result, the model performs too well on the training data sample but fails to perform on new, unseen data points. In the traditional method, datasets are divided into three parts: ***training, validation, and testing.*** 60% data for training, 20% data for validation, and 20% for testing. The training sample helps ***train*** the model, validation helps ***fine-tune*** the model, and the testing set checks the unbiased performance of the model. ***Cross-validation*** is a technique to check the performance of a machine learning model on new or unseen data points. Instead of testing the model on just one split of data, it repeats the process multiple times to get a reliable idea of the model’s performance. 1. **k-Fold Cross-validation:** Divide data into ***k folds***, train on ***k-1 folds,*** test on ***1 fold,*** repeat k times. 2. **Leave-one-out Cross-validation (LOOCV):** Each data point is used once as a test sample, and the rest are used for training. 3. **Holdout Method:** This type of validation splits the dataset randomly into training and testing sets, usually once, but it can be repeated multiple times. It discourages the model from becoming unnecessarily complex, because a complex model may perform well on training but fail on new data points. It pushes the model to learn in a simpler way; it may not perform as well on training data, but it performs better on new data. * **Early Stopping:** We can limit the time the model spends learning from data instead of letting it memorize every data point. It also increases the chances of overfitting because of the complexity; the model can start memorizing the data instead of understanding the hidden patterns or logic. It occurs when the model is too simple and does not learn the patterns or logic in the training data. If the model is not performing well even on the training data, it clearly means that the model is underfit.

results.title: Techniques to Avoid Overfitting
results.content: It fails to perform well in another data set or to predict **future data**. For algorithmic trading, overfitting occurs because a fine-tuned algorithm uses models and parameter values that increase the test performance in the sample by randomness. Each has better performance on the in-sample data compared to the previous version because of added rules. The first two versions of the algorithm perform well with positive return on out-of-sample data despite the acceptable difference in performance compared to the in-sample data. **Split the Data Into Training and Validation Sets** After splitting the data set, we only use the training set to optimize the algorithm’s performance. The validation set is to find a version on the optimization path with a reasonable fit to ensure equivalent performance on both data sets (Figure 12). If a version performs well on both data sets, it’s likely the hidden pattern has been found, and the correct rules and parameters have been identified. In Table 3, using out-of-sample data as a validation set, we can select version 2 as the reasonable fit. **Choose a Simple Preliminary Algorithm to Start With** When an expert proposes a preliminary algorithm to test on the target market, there will be a set of multiple versions that can be applied. These versions are basic algorithms but have different enhancement rules and parameter values. During the optimization process, these versions are tested to find the most likely version that can perform well in the real market. If the preliminary algorithm is simple enough, these versions will have a lesser chance of overfitting. **Drop the Preliminary Algorithm if There Are Too Few Versions for Profit** After evaluating different versions of the initial algorithm, if there are too few instances that  profits, the algorithm hypothesis may not be valid for the target market. The few versions with positive performance may be due to randomness or overfitting of the training data. A process of finding the values of parameters for a trading algorithm to produce the best performance in the target market. The phenomenon that the post-optimization algorithm gives good results on in-sample historical data but performs poorly on unseen out-of-sample data.

results.content: # How to Measure Overfitting When Train and Validation Sample is Small in Keras Model using R. Overfitting is a common challenge in machine learning, where a model learns not only the underlying patterns in the training data but also the noise and details that are not relevant to the generalization of the model. This results in a model that performs well on the training data but poorly on unseen or validation data, as it fails to generalize to new inputs. Overfitting particularly happens in the case of small datasets, where the limited data makes it easier for the model to memorize specific details rather than learning the broader patterns in the R Programming Language. Working with small training and validation datasets in machine learning has many challenges and limitations that can affect model performance. Here are the some of the Main problems which occur to Measure Overfitting When Train and Validation Sample is Small in Keras Model using R. With small datasets, the gap between training and validation loss may be misleading due to limited validation samples. for this Plot training and validation loss over epochs to detect overfitting. # Split data into training and validation sets. # Fit the model with validation data. # Plot training and validation loss. Learning curves might not reveal overfitting if the training data is too small.for this Train the model on increasingly larger subsets of data and plot performance. # Split data into training and validation sets. # Fit the model with validation data. # Plot training and validation loss. Penalize large weights by adding an L2 penalty to the loss function which discards the model from fitting too closely to the training data. # Fit the model with training and validation data. Use K-Fold Cross-Validation to assess model performance across multiple splits of the dataset, reducing the impact of overfitting by averaging performance across different data subsets. When working with small datasets, it is important to carefully evaluate and monitor your model to avoid overfitting, which can lead to poor generalization on new data. Using strategies such as data augmentation, regularization techniques, early stopping, and cross-validation can enhance model performance and robustness. ## Deep Learning Models.
